reasoning: Applies rules already in this lesson in the order a technician meets them: FSP-009 (eliminate or minimise risk), FSP-011 (site release), FSP-012/FSP-016 (RCD), FSP-025 (licensed electrician), FSP-087 (wet methods smear dry soot), FSP-126/FSP-039 (build-date asbestos rule). Inherits the open GAPs FSP-011, FSP-025 and FSP-087 and resolves with them.

claim: Australian health advice is to avoid evaporative coolers during smoke because they bring outside air inside.
quote: avoid using evaporative coolers, as they bring outside air inside.

claim: An evaporative cooler in use can replace all the air in a house every 2 to 3 minutes.
quote: When in use, evaporative coolers can completely replace the air in the house every 2 to 3 minutes.

claim: Ash can still enter a home with doors and windows closed and heating or cooling off, through cracked cornices, unsealed fans and vents, ceiling roses and gaps around doors and windows.
quote: Even though you may have closed your doors and windows and turned off any cooling or heating systems, ash can still come into the home

claim: Cobargo house: 180 m² x 2.4 m = 432 m³; one change every 3 minutes = 20 changes an hour, about 8,640 m³ of outside air an hour.
reasoning: Illustrative figures (labelled in the lesson). 180 x 2.4 = 432; 60 / 3 = 20; 432 x 20 = 8,640. The 2-to-3-minute rate is FSP-131.

claim: In a mixed-use or strata building, authority to survey and scope comes from each owner or tenancy and, for common property, the strata company or owners corporation; set the boundary floor by floor.
reasoning: Extends the rule already taught in this lesson (adjoining units need their own owner's authority) to common property, which strata law in each state and territory, and the Unit Titles Act 2010 in New Zealand, places with the body corporate. The floor-by-floor boundary applies FSP-036. SME to confirm wording.

claim: NSW EPA: do not enter a property after a bushfire until emergency services or the local council confirm it is safe.
quote: Do not enter your property after a bushfire until emergency services or your local council confirm it is safe.

claim: SafeWork NSW: bushfire-affected properties can have downed live power lines, active solar panels and hot coals hidden under rubble.
quote: electrical hazards could exist such as live power lines that may be down or active solar panels

claim: NSW: depending on severity, NSW Public Works, the EPA or the local council may assess fire-affected properties and put controls in place.
quote: NSW Public Works, the NSW Environment Protection Authority (EPA) and/or local council may assess the fire-impacted properties and implement controls

claim: NSW EPA: clean-up may start with a safety assessment of nearby properties, so asbestos fibres are not spread during the work.
quote: This might include prioritising a safety assessment of properties in close proximity, to minimise the risk of asbestos fibres being spread during clean-up work.

claim: WorkSafe Victoria: bushfire-affected asbestos that cannot be accessed is treated as friable and needs a Class A licence holder.
quote: if all bushfire impacted ACM is not accessible it needs to be treated as friable

claim: WorkSafe Victoria: where a competent person finds bushfire-affected ACM has stayed non-friable, a Class B licence holder may remove it.
quote: the ACM remains in its non-friable state, then the removal work may be carried out by a Class B asbestos removal licence holder.

claim: WorkSafe Victoria: asbestos samples from a bushfire site are analysed by a NATA-accredited laboratory.
quote: analysis of samples must be undertaken by a laboratory accredited by the National Association of Testing Authorities (NATA).

claim: The Victorian Government may appoint a clean-up contractor for bushfire-destroyed properties.
quote: The Victorian Government may appoint a contractor as a clean-up provider for bushfire destroyed properties.

claim: WorkSafe NZ: damaged asbestos-containing materials are less dangerous while wet but can release fibres once dry.
quote: When damaged asbestos-containing materials are wet, they are not as dangerous, but once dry they can cause a risk to health

claim: WorkSafe NZ: contact a licensed asbestos assessor or removalist before a damaged structure presumed to contain asbestos is reoccupied.
quote: If the damaged structure is presumed to be asbestos containing, a licensed asbestos assessor or licensed asbestos removalist should also be contacted before reoccupation.

claim: NSW EPA: avoid spreading ash or debris and do not use a broom.
quote: Avoid spreading ash or debris around your property. Do not use a broom.

claim: EPA Victoria: do not use leaf blowers or anything that pushes ash into the air.
quote: avoid getting ash in the air as much as possible – don’t use leaf blowers or anything that will push the ash into the air

claim: NSW EPA: dampen ash with water to minimise dust, but do not use high-pressure water spray.
quote: Dampen ash with water to minimise dust but don’t use high pressure water spray.

claim: SafeWork NSW: dust suppression should not be so heavy that it runs off into nearby drains and waterways.
quote: Dust suppression should not be so great that it causes runoff into nearby drains and waterways.

claim: NSW EPA: do not bury building rubble, as it may contain hazardous materials.
quote: Do not bury building rubble as it may contain hazardous materials.

claim: NSW EPA: remove protective gear before leaving, seal it in a heavy-duty 0.2 mm plastic bag and dispose of it as asbestos waste.
quote: place it in a heavy duty (0.2 mm) plastic bag, seal it and dispose of it as asbestos waste.

claim: Blue Mountains scenario: neighbour's fragments on the client's land are treated as fire-damaged and friable (Class A); a 1998 house is suspect because it predates the 2003 ban; the crew's route must not cross the debris.
reasoning: Applies FSP-043 (NSW: fire-impacted ACM is friable, Class A), FSP-126 (assume asbestos before the 31 December 2003 ban; pre-1990 most likely) and FSP-052 (stop, isolate, hand over) to an illustrative bushfire scenario. Inherits GAP FSP-052 for the restorer's stop-isolate step.

claim: SafeWork NSW: bushfire debris can contain asbestos, ash from burnt CCA-treated timber, medicines, chemicals, damaged gas bottles and metal residues from burnt appliances.
quote: Hazardous household materials that may be present after a bushfire include asbestos, ash from burnt treated timbers (i.e. copper chrome arsenate or CCA), medicines

claim: SafeWork NSW: do not use paper dust masks, handkerchiefs or bandannas; P2 masks are the minimum for fine particles including asbestos fibres.
quote: Do not use ordinary paper dust masks, handkerchiefs or bandannas. Face masks (called ‘P2 masks’) should be worn, as a minimum

claim: Toowoomba fence scenario: paling and pergola ash treated as CCA ash; a 1984 house in Australia is tested for lead before stripping (presumed in NZ); fibre-cement eaves from 1984 sit inside the most likely asbestos period.
reasoning: Applies FSP-066/FSP-068/FSP-069 (CCA ash handling), FSP-054 (AU lead before 1970, newer homes may still have it), FSP-055 (NZ presume lead for 1980s or earlier), FSP-059 (no open flame on lead paint) and FSP-038/FSP-126 (asbestos build dates) to an illustrative scenario.

claim: Judge a test patch only when dry; a patch that dries with a ring or a gloss change has failed.
reason: CARSI field-method wording with no public source found. SME to confirm against field practice and the licensed standard (read by a person, not an AI tool).

claim: Office ceiling: 1.2 m x 0.6 m = 0.72 m² per tile; 600 m² / 0.72 is about 833 tiles; a quarter is about 208 tiles, about 150 m².
reasoning: Illustrative figures (labelled in the lesson). 1.2 x 0.6 = 0.72; 600 / 0.72 = 833.3; 833 / 4 = 208.25; 208 x 0.72 = 149.8.

claim: Opening doors to air a room when the outside air is as humid as the inside works against the dehumidifier.
reasoning: Psychrometric reasoning: a dehumidifier lowers the moisture content of the room air; exchanging it with outside air at the same or higher moisture content (g/kg) replaces dried air with moist air. Consistent with FSP-095 (lower RH slows corrosion), which remains GAP.

claim: EPA Victoria: have HVAC units and all ductwork professionally cleaned and filters replaced to remove soot, ash and smoke residue.
quote: Have heating, ventilating and air-conditioning units and all ductwork professionally cleaned and replace filters, to remove soot, ash and smoke residue.

claim: EPA Victoria: wash soft furnishings or vacuum them with a HEPA-filtered vacuum so particles do not blow back into the house.
quote: vacuum using a vacuum with a HEPA filter, so particles don’t blow back into your house.

claim: NSW Health: humidifiers, negative ion generators and odour absorbers do not remove fine particles in bushfire smoke.
quote: Humidifiers, negative ion generators and odour absorbers do not remove fine particles in bushfire smoke.

claim: Verification includes a clean white-cloth wipe test of surfaces, recorded area by area.
